item.title: Book spells
item.description: Stanford Events — Boil, boil, toil and trouble… what bewitching book will you find at the Education Library? Our witchy book display has a little bit of magic for everyone! Meet witches who are mischievous, adventurous, and sometimes downright wicked. From little witches who aren’t too scary to cooking witches (spoiler alert the frog lives!) and skin shedding fireball witches for older readers, there’s plenty here to scare up a good read. So come to the Education Library, pick a book, and see if you can find a story that puts you under its spell! Location: Education (Cubberley Bldg)

item.title: Carolyn Lazard: Long Take
item.description: Stanford Events — Carolyn Lazard: Long Take is a multimedia exhibition that begins with a score for a performance and unfolds as a series of interventions that engage accessibility as an artistic material. Made in collaboration with dancer Jerron Herman and poet and artist Joselia Rebekah Hughes, the central work, Leans, Reverses (2022), emerges from the relationship between a dance performance, its recording, and transcription (a choreographic score, captions, and audio description). The installation includes two additional works which are created anew at each showing based on the artist’s instructions. Institutional Seat (2022) modifies a standard bench from the museum’s galleries into a version that is more comfortable for all museum visitors. Surround Sound (2022) attends to the floor of the gallery with dance-floor materials. Over the course of the exhibition, this floor will collect marks made by visitors’ shoes, strollers, and wheelchair treads, like another form of tally or notation. Carolyn Laz

item.title: JANE! An intimate exploration of Gilded Age excess and the enigmatic life and death of Jane Stanford
item.description: Stanford Events — Curated by Associate Curator of European Art, Patrick R. Crowley, JANE! celebrates the aesthetic and affective excesses of Jane Stanford, the Gilded Age founder and matriarch of Stanford University. Bringing together precious keepsakes, souvenirs, archaeological detritus, and spooky messages from beyond the grave, the exhibition reveals the campy underside of a familiar biography and perhaps an even more familiar murder mystery. From her elegant French gowns to a colossal painting of her jewels, from the Egyptian artifacts she acquired for her fledgling museum to a Hawaiian skirt she may or may not have purchased immediately before her suspicious death, Jane! presents various idiosyncratic artifacts of Stanford lore—many shown for the very first time, and very likely for the last. IMAGE: Napoleon T. Sarony, Portrait of Jane Lathrop Stanford, 1871. Photograph with charcoal touch up, 55 ½ x 45 in. Cantor Arts Center, Stanford University, Stanford Family Collections, JLS.18217 MUSEUM HOUR

item.description: Stanford Events — The East Asia Library at Stanford University will host a print exhibition by Kim Bong-Jun, a leading figure in Korean Minjung (People’s) Art, from September 29 to December 11, 2026. Active since the 1980s, Kim has developed a distinctive visual language that combines traditional Korean folk art and popular expression with contemporary art, reflecting the lives and realities of ordinary people and envisioning possibilities for a more just and ecological future. The exhibition explores Kim’s concept of “Indigenous Futures” through art as a form of civilizational transformation, expressing p'owŏl (포월 抱越), embracing and transcending the pain and contradictions of reality while reaching toward new possibilities for the future. The opening reception on October 8 will feature an artist talk and a Korean mask dance (탈춤 t'alch'um) performance by Kim Bong-Jun and Che Se-hyun, a Seattle-based creative director and multidisciplinary artist. item.title: Solid Pictures: Photosculpture and the Making of Modern Likeness
item.description: Stanford Events — Before 3D printing, there was photosculpture. Curated by Patrick R. Crowley, Associate Curator of European Art, Solid Pictures is the first major exhibition to explore these largely overlooked objects first conceived in 1859 by the twenty-nine-year-old French artist and inventor François Willème. Employing projection technologies and mechanical instruments, Willème and his team of operators translated photographic negatives into solid figures across a variety of media, aiming to create affordable portrait sculpture for the burgeoning middle class of Second Empire France. Though commercially unsuccessful, these experiments laid the groundwork for the scanning, machining, and printing technologies ubiquitous today. Bringing together these rare artifacts, the exhibition opens up a little-known chapter of history to reveal the roots and richness of our contemporary world. item.title: Text Machines: Scarlet Thread of the Digital Order (1883-2026)
item.description: Stanford Events — Stanford Libraries now holds an 1883 edition of a rare book, Les laboureurs: poème tiré de Jocelyn, whose pages (text and ornaments) were entirely woven on a Jacquard loom by the firm of silk merchant Joseph-Alphonse Henry. This exhibition explores the cultural contexts and material conditions of Les laboureurs’ production, and considers parallels between technology-driven global change in the late nineteenth century and in our current day. The exhibition includes microscope images revealing the textile structure of the woven text as well as a woven enlargement that illustrates its basic principles, along with several artworks inspired by or related to the themes of the exhibition. Location: Green Library, Bing Wing

item.title: Electric Contrasts: the Art of the Detail
item.description: Stanford Events — Electric Contrasts: The Art of the Detail brings together photobooks and magazines to show how the revolution of photography in the late 19th and early 20th century changed the history of art. Electric Contrasts takes Kenneth Clark’s landmark 1938 book One Hundred Details from Pictures in the National Gallery as a starting point to illuminate the impact black and white photographic details of Old Master paintings had on new ways of seeing in the early 20th century. The exhibition reveals the anachronistic and provocative juxtapositions of artworks in avant-garde magazines and books which created a radically new vision that would go on to influence television and the internet. Curated by Altair Brandon-Salmon. Bowes Art & Architecture Library hours: M-Th 9-7pm; Friday 9-5pm; Sunday 12-6pm. Tour by Dr. Brandon-Salmon on 9/5 at 6 pm prior to Electric Contrasts Study Evening. Location: McMurtry Building

item.title: The Alliance for Civics in the Academy discussing Civics Programs And Their Critics
item.description: Stanford Events — The recent resurgence in postsecondary civic education has been anchored by a proliferation of new civics centers across the country. These centers have attracted attention, funding, and critics who question their political independence and their place in faculty governance. On this month's episode of Civics in the Academy, our panelists will explore the arguments for and against the role of these centers in the civics ecosystem. The Alliance for Civics in the Academy held "Civics Programs and their Critics" with John von Heyking, Anthony Ives, Hollis Robbins, and Joseph Knippenberg on October 29, 2026, from 9:00-10:00 a.m. PT. The Civics in the Academy webinar series features in-depth discussions on the practice, pedagogy, and state of civics in higher education. Drawing on the diverse expertise and perspectives within the Alliance network, each session features topics and panelists sourced directly from our membership. item.title: Benjamin Yoel — International Pressure and Opposition to Democratic Backsliding
item.description: Stanford Events — Under what conditions do pro-democracy global actors support domestic opposition actors resisting democratic backsliding, and when does such support shape public opinion? This book project develops a theory of international rhetorical pressure that examines both the supply and demand of foreign engagement in backsliding contexts. On the supply side, it argues that international actors' public attention to democratic developments abroad is shaped by both domestic political developments and geopolitical ties. On the demand side, it suggests that foreign statements can shape public opinion toward pro-democracy movements. Drawing on an original dataset of US Secretary of State speeches, survey experiments, and elite interviews, the project shows that geopolitical interests often shape when international actors publicly address democracy abroad, but that when they do, foreign messages can meaningfully shape public opinion. item.title: Film Screening of the 2026 Lithuanian submission for the Academy Awards – How to Divorce During the War
item.description: Stanford Events — Join us for a film screening of Lithuania's submission for the Academy Awards with commentary from Maarja Merivoo-Parro, CEO of Vabamu Museum of Occupations and Freedom. How to Divorce During the War takes place in Vilnius, Lithuania in 2022. High-flying executive, Marija (Zygimante Elena Jakstaite), chooses the worst possible moment to inform her husband, Vytas (Marius Repsys), that she wants a divorce: just one day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Suddenly the couple must navigate the process of separation as it collides with a refugee and mid-life crisis. A struggling film director, Vytas is put into a tight spot by having to move in with his Russophile parents, while Marija struggles to find her footing as the war affects both her business and home life. As the reason for the divorce gradually becomes clear, the dissolution of Marija and Vytas’ marriage creates conflicts and opportunities for both of them, while also affecting their ever-observant young daughter, Dovile. item.title: Book Talk: Chrystia Freeland — Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider’s View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People
item.description: Stanford Events — How should allies deal with a superpower they can no longer rely on? Former Canadian Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland joins CDDRL to discuss her new book, "Unreliable Boyfriend: An Insider's View of Dealing with a Chaotic Superpower, Plutocrats, and Other Complicated People." Freeland has seen these questions from two sides. As a foreign correspondent, she covered the rise of Russia's oligarchs in the 1990s. As a senior Canadian official, she helped renegotiate the trade agreement between Canada, the U.S. and Mexico. The book draws on both careers to examine how power operates inside government, why trade, security and democracy can no longer be treated separately, and how democracies might build coalitions strong enough to resist authoritarian states and domestic oligarchs. item.title: Book Talk — We Shall Outlast Them: Putin’s Global Campaign to Defeat the West
item.description: Stanford Events — How has Russia sustained its confrontation with the West since 2022, and at what cost? In her new book, Hanna Notte argues the Kremlin is waging a war not only on Ukraine but over the global order itself. Notte traces how Russia adapted after the invasion. It worked around sanctions, built new partnerships, cultivated support across the Global South and tried to deepen divisions within Western democracies. Her account combines policy analysis with field reporting from more than a dozen countries and interviews with officials, facilitators and ordinary people drawn into Russia's agenda. The book also examines the domestic consequences. Notte finds that Putin's focus on confronting the West has distorted Russia's economy and moved the country from a tacit dictatorship toward a full one. She suggests Putin may outlast the West, but has gambled Russia's future in the process. item.title: Planetary Science and Exploration Seminar, Catherine Johnson - "Mercury’s Enigmatic Magnetic Field"
item.description: Stanford Events — Mercury’s interior structure and its magnetic field are unique among the terrestrial planets and moons of the Solar System. Its large metallic core (~83% of the planetary radius) formed under highly reducing conditions, requiring a core composition that includes substantial silicon and some, but more limited, sulfur and carbon. Mercury is also the only planet other than Earth to have both core and crustal magnetic fields. The core field constrains the present-day dynamo and crustal magnetization, if remanent, can constrain the dynamo history. The core field is dominantly dipolar, axisymmetric, asymmetric about the planetary equator, and ~100 times weaker than Earth’s field at the planetary surface. Structure beyond this simple picture is weak but exists, in particular a high-northern-latitude regional magnetic field anomaly spatially coincident with the topographic and gravity signature of Mercury’s Northern Rise. item.description: Stanford Events — The Girand Center for Biomedical Ethics is pleased to announce this year’s speaker, Dr. Bryant Lin, in conversation with Dr. Shoshana Ungerleider, for the 36th Annual Jonathan J. King Lecture. item.title: Stanford Energy Seminar | Soft Materials for Hard Sustainability Challenges: Water production, Data center Sustainability, and High-Temperature Heat | Carlos Diaz-Marin, Stanford University
item.description: Stanford Events — The Stanford Energy Seminar has been a mainstay of energy engagement at Stanford for nearly 20 years and is one of the flagship programs of the Precourt Institute for Energy. We aim to bring a wide variety of perspectives to the Stanford community – academics, entrepreneurs, utilities, non-profits, and more. About the talk Water scarcity, rising energy demand, and global emissions are major sustainability challenges of the 21st century. This talk will highlight three soft matter-enabled technologies that the Diaz-Marin lab is developing to tackle these challenges. First, he will present their multiscale design of hydrogel-salt composites to produce water from air in any geography and at costs comparable to those of tap water. Secondly, he will show how low temperature carbon capture sorbents could transform AI into carbon-negative and water-positive by enabling data center heat reuse for carbon removal.
